human_tolerance.notes: Ubiquitous in urban areas all over Australia and accustomed to people; a familiar bird of parks, gardens, golf courses, streets and farmland, so long as scattered trees are nearby for nesting and shelter.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: Long breeding season varying across the range: June-September in northern Australia, commencing August-September in cooler regions and continuing until January in some alpine areas. The nest is a bowl of sticks built by the female high in a tree fork; clutch of two to five eggs, incubation around 20 days.

phases.name: territorial
phases.note: Sedentary and territorial throughout the range; groups occupy and defend the same territory for much of the year, with peak defensive (swooping) behaviour during the breeding season, late August to late November in most regions.

vocalizations.description: A loud, musical, complex warbling carol of 4-5 slurred elements pitched at 6-8 kHz, given by pairs (sometimes whole groups) to advertise and defend territory; often preceded by quieter warbling, with a short repetitive dawn song just before dawn and a dusk song at twilight in winter and spring.
High-pitched (8-10 kHz) alarm or rallying calls given when intruders or threats are spotted; sentinel birds rally the group to coordinated mobbing of raptors and other predators.
A repeated short, loud (around 80 dB), high-pitched (8 kHz) begging call emitted by fledglings and juveniles.

taxonomy.note: GBIF backbone match (usageKey 2489450, EXACT, confidence 99) gives family Cracticidae; Wikipedia notes the Australian magpie is placed in Artamidae by recent authors, with Cracticidae used following the GBIF backbone. Authority 'Latham, 1802' as the GBIF backbone gives it (Wikipedia says the species was first described by Latham in 1801 as Coracias tibicen).

external.note: GBIF usageKey 2489450 and iNaturalist taxon 8575 as given in the issue's data pointers and confirmed by the GBIF match API; ITIS TSN 560338, NCBI 9132, eBird ausmag2, MDD 61731 and Wikidata Q1140949 via Wikidata (P815, P685, P3444, P10585, P846, P3151).

conservation.note: Wikidata P141 = Q211005 (IUCN Red List category Least Concern).

range.note: Native to Australia and the Trans-Fly region of southern New Guinea; introduced to New Zealand (1860s-1874), Fiji (Taveuni) and the Solomon Islands. A Sri Lanka introduction failed to establish and is not listed.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: Walk and Fly only: the source states the Australian magpie 'moves around by walking, and is the only member of the Artamidae to do so; woodswallows, butcherbirds and currawongs all tend to hop with legs parallel', and that with its long legs it 'walks rather than waddles or hops'. The issue recipe suggested copying pica-pica's Walk/Hop/Fly set, but the source is explicit that this species walks rather than hops, so Hop was dropped.

traits.nest_type.note: Judgement mapping: the source describes 'a bowl-shaped structure made of sticks and lined with softer material such as grass and bark' built high in a tree fork; the schema's enum (Cup/Cavity/Platform/Ground/Burrow/None) has no stick-bowl option, so 'Platform' was chosen as the closest fit, as for the Eurasian magpie.

traits.perching.note: Nests and shelters in trees; a perching passerine.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg (0.285 kg); the validator's size-class bands place this in the Small band (< 1 kg).

traits.mass_kg.note: Midpoint of the 220-350 g adult range given in the Description section.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: Adult mass 220-350 g as stated in the Description section.

traits.length_m.note: Midpoint of 37-43 cm adult length (Description section).

traits.wingspan_m.note: Midpoint of the 65-85 cm wingspan given in the Description section.

traits.lifespan_y.note: 'Australian magpies generally live to around 25 years of age, though ages of up to 30 years have been recorded.'

traits.diet.note: Judgement: no sourced percentages were found. The Feeding section lists diet items qualitatively ('omnivorous... invertebrates such as earthworms, millipedes, snails, spiders and scorpions as well as a wide variety of insects... Skinks, frogs, small birds, mice and other small animals as well as carrion, grain, tubers, figs and walnuts') and states the bulk of the diet is invertebrates; shares were authored to reflect that ordering (invertebrates largest, then small vertebrates, mast/seed, carrion, fruit).

traits.social.note: 'living in groups occupying a territory, or in flocks or fringe groups', with cooperative breeding helpers assisting in feeding young; group size is not numerically stated in the source, so the 2-8 range is judgement (a pair plus helpers up to a small flock).

traits.activity_pattern.note: 'The Australian magpie is almost exclusively diurnal, although it may call into the night.'

traits.defense.note: Coordinated mobbing of raptors ('sentinel birds and subsequent coordinated mobbing of the intruder... harass and drive the raptor to some distance beyond the territory') and well-documented swooping attacks on people during the breeding season; Mob is a better fit than Flee for this species.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement: magpies are ubiquitous in urban Australia and accustomed to people ('have become accustomed to people'), regularly fed by households, yet a minority become aggressively swooping in spring and the species is generally wary of strangers; a mid-range wariness was authored.

habitat.use.note: Judgement split: the source states birds 'forage mainly on the ground in these open areas' but 'nest and shelter in trees', with no numeric split given.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: Nests and shelters in trees (often high in a tree fork); tagged as 'perch' shelter.

habitat.resources.note: Invertebrates (bulk of diet), small vertebrates (skinks, frogs, small birds, mice), carrion, mast (grain, tubers, walnuts), seed and fruit (figs) from the Feeding section; nest_platform and perch/shelter from the Breeding and Distribution sections. Weights are judgement, not separately sourced percentages.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: 'Magpies are ubiquitous in urban areas all over Australia, and have become accustomed to people'; 'adapted well to human habitation and is a familiar bird of parks, gardens and farmland'. flight_distance_m and light_max are judgement (not separately sourced numbers).

seasonal.strategy.note: 'The magpie is generally sedentary and territorial throughout its range'; no migration described, so ActiveYearRound.

seasonal.phases.note: Breeding window June to January spans the regional variation given in the Breeding section (June-September in the north, from August-September in cooler regions, to January in alpine areas); territoriality is year-round with peak swooping defence from late August to late November. Exact day-of-month boundaries are judgement.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Egg (clutch of two to five, incubation around 20 days), altricial juvenile (hatches naked and blind, eyes open ~10 days, begins foraging at three weeks, mostly feeding itself by six months) and adult (adult size by first year, first breeding at three to five years); no sourced juvenile-plumage duration was found so duration_days/scale were left unset.

vocalizations.carolling.note: 'Its complex, musical, warbling call is one of the most familiar Australian bird sounds'; carolling 'pitched between 6 and 8 kHz and has 4-5 elements with slurring indistinct noise in between', with a dawn song just before dawn and a dusk song at twilight in winter and spring (austral winter-spring, June-November).

vocalizations.rallying.note: 'They employ several high pitched (8-10 kHz) alarm or rallying calls when intruders or threats are spotted.'

vocalizations.begging.note: 'Fledgling and juvenile magpies emit a repeated short and loud (80 dB), high-pitched (8 kHz) begging call'; season_months aligned to the breeding window as a judgement.

look.note: Glossy black head, wings and underparts with white shoulders and nape, black tail with a black terminal band, bluish-white wedge-shaped bill bordered with black, black legs, and gold-brown eyes in adults. Palette approximates this with a near-black body, white 'markings' on the outer wing (shoulder) parts, a bluish-white 'accent' beak and a gold-brown eye; the breast is black (not white), so it is pinned to the body slot. Proportions (robust body, long strong legs, longish tail) are authored judgement.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared perching-songbird program, following the issue recipe: song and alarm point at the carolling and rallying calls; food_tag invertebrate reflects the bulk of the diet; nest months kept at the program's spring default as authored values.
